key_results: A period-N discrete-time sequence requires only N distinct harmonically related complex exponentials because frequency indices separated by N generate identical sequences. The DFS synthesis equation uses those N basis functions, and the analysis equation follows from their finite-sum orthogonality. [§8.1, Eqs. 8.1–8.12]

DFS coefficients and periodic sequences are both period N. Linearity, circular time shift, duality, conjugate/even/odd symmetries, and periodic convolution form the core algebra; periodic convolution in time corresponds to pointwise multiplication of DFS coefficients. [§§8.2.1–8.2.6, Table 8.1]

The Fourier transform of a periodic sequence is an impulse train in frequency whose weights are proportional to the sequence’s DFS coefficients; conversely, the DFS coefficients are equally spaced samples of the Fourier transform of one period. [§8.3, Eqs. 8.40–8.48]

Sampling X(e^{jω}) at N equally spaced frequencies, equivalently sampling X(z) at N equally spaced unit-circle points, produces a period-N sequence whose inverse DFS is the sum of time-shifted replicas Σ_r x[n−rN]. If the replicas overlap, frequency-domain undersampling appears as time-domain aliasing. [§8.4, Eqs. 8.49–8.57, Figs. 8.7–8.9]

The N-point DFT of a finite sequence is one period of the DFS coefficients of its periodic extension and is equal to samples of its DTFT/z-transform at z=e^{j2πk/N}; the inverse DFT reconstructs one period. The representation therefore carries an implicit periodicity even when the original sequence is treated as finite. [§8.5, Eqs. 8.58–8.68]

DFT properties are DFS properties interpreted on finite-length representatives: time shifts are circular, products correspond to circular convolution, and symmetry for real sequences permits one half of the spectrum to determine the other half. [§§8.6.1–8.6.6, Table 8.2]

The linear convolution of length-L and length-P sequences has maximum length L+P−1. An N-point circular convolution equals that linear convolution without time aliasing when N≥L+P−1; otherwise the excess tail wraps onto earlier samples. [§§8.7.1–8.7.2, Eqs. 8.129–8.139, Figs. 8.17–8.21]

An indefinitely long LTI filtering problem with a finite impulse response can be decomposed into blocks and evaluated by DFT multiplication using overlap-add or overlap-save, choosing transform length so circular convolution reproduces the required linear-convolution samples. [§8.7.3, Figs. 8.22–8.24]

DCT variants arise from different even periodic extensions of a real finite sequence. The DCT-1 corresponds to Type-1 symmetry with period 2N−2; the DCT-2 corresponds to half-sample Type-2 symmetry with period 2N. Both can be computed through related DFTs. [§§8.8.1–8.8.4, Eqs. 8.150–8.175, Figs. 8.25–8.26]

The DCT-2 often compacts correlated signal energy into low-index coefficients more strongly than the DFT, which is why it is central to transform coding. Symmetric extension also reduces objectionable endpoint discontinuities and blocking artifacts in image filtering. [§§8.8.5–8.8.6, Eqs. 8.176–8.180, Figs. 8.27–8.29]

Direct evaluation of an N-point complex DFT costs on the order of N² operations; FFT algorithms exploit twiddle-factor symmetry and periodicity by recursively decomposing the transform, reducing computation to order N log₂N for power-of-two lengths. [§§9.0–9.1]

The Goertzel algorithm evaluates a selected Fourier-transform/DFT value as the terminal output of a second-order real-coefficient recursion plus a final zero operation. Computing M selected values costs order NM and can beat a full FFT when M is smaller than roughly log₂N. [§9.2, Eqs. 9.4–9.9, Figs. 9.1–9.2]

Radix-2 decimation in time splits the input into even- and odd-indexed subsequences and recursively combines their DFTs with butterflies. There are log₂N stages; the unoptimized flow graph uses N log₂N complex multiplications/additions, with further savings from twiddle symmetry. [§9.3, Eqs. 9.10–9.19, Figs. 9.3–9.10]

Radix-2 decimation in frequency instead decomposes the output-frequency indices. DIT and DIF have comparable arithmetic but complementary ordering: common in-place forms place either input or output in bit-reversed order. [§§9.3.1–9.4.2, Figs. 9.11–9.24]

In-place butterflies overwrite arrays without losing needed data, reducing storage to N complex values; practical implementations must coordinate bit-reversed indexing, stage-dependent butterfly spacing, and coefficient access order. [§§9.3.1, 9.5.1–9.5.2]

Composite transform lengths can be factored into mixed-radix Cooley–Tukey decompositions; relatively prime factors enable prime-factor algorithms that exchange more complex indexing for fewer multiplications. [§9.5.3]

The Winograd Fourier transform rewrites short relatively-prime DFTs as periodic convolutions and can make multiplication count proportional to N rather than N log N, but its additions, bookkeeping, and separate multiplication/accumulation requirements can outweigh that benefit on general processors. [§9.6.1]

The chirp transform rewrites arbitrary equally spaced samples of a Fourier transform as a convolution between chirp-modulated data and a chirp impulse response. Its generalized chirp z-transform evaluates points equally spaced in angle on a spiral z-plane contour. [§9.6.2, Eqs. 9.37–9.52, Figs. 9.25–9.31]

In a fixed-point radix-2 FFT, an additive-noise model gives output noise power proportional to N before scaling. Scaling the input once to guarantee no overflow makes noise-to-signal ratio grow as N² (about one bit per stage); scaling by 1/2 at every stage improves the growth to N (about half a bit per stage). [§9.7, Eqs. 9.53–9.69, Figs. 9.32–9.36]

Block floating point normalizes the array, tests overflow during the FFT, shifts the whole array when necessary, and records a shared scale factor; floating point avoids forced stage scaling and makes noise growth with transform length substantially milder. [§9.7]

DFT-based Fourier analysis of a continuous signal comprises antialias filtering, sampling, finite windowing, and frequency sampling. For a sampling interval T and N-point DFT, bin k corresponds to continuous angular frequency 2πk/(NT), subject to periodic negative-frequency interpretation. [§10.1, Eqs. 10.1–10.5, Figs. 10.1–10.2]

Multiplying by a finite window convolves the true spectrum with the window spectrum. Main-lobe width controls the ability to resolve nearby sinusoids, while sidelobe level controls leakage; rectangular windows give narrow main lobes but high sidelobes, and Kaiser parameters explicitly trade length, main-lobe width, and sidelobe suppression. [§10.2.1, Eqs. 10.6–10.14, Figs. 10.3–10.4]

DFT spectral sampling can miss or misstate peaks that lie between bins. Zero-padding a fixed window increases the density of spectral samples and interpolates the same windowed spectrum but does not improve resolution; only increasing the observation/window length narrows the main lobe and resolves closer components. [§10.2.2, Examples 10.4–10.8, Figs. 10.5–10.10]

The time-dependent or short-time Fourier transform converts a sequence into a time–frequency function by transforming windowed neighborhoods. It is invertible when the window includes a nonzero reference sample and can equivalently be viewed as a bank of frequency-shifted versions of the window response. [§10.3, Eqs. 10.18–10.28, Figs. 10.11–10.14]

Short windows improve time localization but broaden the equivalent analysis filters; long windows improve frequency resolution but smear temporal change. With an L-sample window, N frequency samples and time hop R support exact reconstruction when the windowed blocks are fully represented and cover the signal (in the standard construction, N≥L and R≤L). [§§10.3.1–10.3.2, Eqs. 10.29–10.37, Figs. 10.13–10.16]

Overlap-add block convolution is a special use of the sampled time-dependent Fourier transform: modify each block spectrum by the filter response, inverse transform, then overlap and add reconstructed blocks. [§10.4, Eqs. 10.38–10.42]

Speech is locally stationary over roughly 30–40 ms: short-window wideband spectrograms reveal timing and vocal-tract formant motion, while long-window narrowband spectrograms resolve harmonic structure. [§10.5.1, Example 10.10, Figs. 10.17–10.18]

For pulse radar, round-trip delay estimates range and Doppler frequency estimates radial velocity. A short-time spectrum tracks changing Doppler peaks when motion is nonuniform, provided the window is short enough for local constant-frequency behavior but long enough to separate multiple returns. [§10.5.2, Eqs. 10.43–10.47, Fig. 10.19]

A (modified) periodogram is the normalized squared magnitude of the Fourier transform of a windowed record and equivalently the Fourier transform of its finite-record autocorrelation. It is nonnegative; after proper normalization it is asymptotically unbiased, but its variance remains approximately the square of the true spectrum, so it is not consistent. [§§10.6.1–10.6.2, Eqs. 10.48–10.66, Figs. 10.20–10.21]

Bartlett/Welch averaging divides a record into windowed segments and averages their periodograms. For K approximately independent segments, variance falls by 1/K; increasing segment length reduces bias but reduces K for a fixed record, creating a bias–variance/resolution tradeoff. Half-window overlap can nearly halve variance again, whereas heavier overlap yields diminishing returns. [§§10.6.3–10.6.4, Eqs. 10.67–10.77]

An alternative spectrum estimate first estimates autocorrelation, windows its reliable low-lag portion, and Fourier transforms it. Shorter lag windows smooth variance at the cost of resolution; nonnegative spectral estimates require a lag window whose Fourier transform is nonnegative. [§10.7, Eqs. 10.82–10.96]

The DFT computes the needed aperiodic autocorrelation by zero-padding a length-Q record and transforming |X[k]|²; to preserve lags 0 through M−1 without circular wrap, choose N≥Q+M−1. FFT evaluation typically becomes advantageous before M reaches about 100. [§10.7.1, Eqs. 10.97–10.99, Fig. 10.24]

A causal real sequence is completely recoverable from its even part; correspondingly, for a causal stable real sequence, either the real or (up to the value at zero) imaginary part of its Fourier transform determines the other through a periodic cotangent-kernel Cauchy-principal-value Hilbert transform. [§11.1, Eqs. 11.1–11.30, Figs. 11.1–11.2]

For an even-N finite sequence supported only through N/2, periodic causality creates finite-sum Hilbert relations between the real and imaginary parts of its DFT. The relations are circular convolutions and can themselves be evaluated efficiently with FFTs. [§11.2, Eqs. 11.31–11.52, Fig. 11.3]

If the complex cepstrum is causal—equivalently, for the minimum-phase case with all poles and zeros inside the unit circle—log magnitude and continuous phase form a Hilbert-transform pair. Magnitude determines phase; phase determines magnitude only up to an overall gain unless the cepstral zero term is known. [§11.3, Eqs. 11.53–11.56]

A discrete-time analytic signal has a spectrum zero on the negative-frequency half of each period. Its real and imaginary components are Hilbert-transform pairs: the ideal transformer has unit magnitude, phase −π/2 for positive frequencies and +π/2 for negative frequencies, and impulse response 2sin²(πn/2)/(πn) for n≠0. [§11.4, Eqs. 11.57–11.66, Figs. 11.4–11.6]

The ideal Hilbert transformer is noncausal and not absolutely summable. Window or equiripple FIR approximations preserve exact 90° phase plus linear delay: Type III has zeros at DC and Nyquist and many zero coefficients, while Type IV is zero only at DC and better covers the Nyquist neighborhood. [§11.4.1, Eqs. 11.67–11.70, Figs. 11.7–11.9]

A complex lowpass analytic signal shifted by e^{jω_cn} gives a one-sided complex bandpass signal. Its real part is an in-phase/quadrature representation and can be written as an amplitude envelope times a phase-modulated carrier, providing the standard basis for single-sideband modulation. [§11.4.2, Eqs. 11.71–11.77, Figs. 11.10–11.11]

A real bandpass signal can be converted to a complex analytic sequence, decimated without overlap according to its occupied bandwidth, processed at the reduced rate, then expanded, complex-bandpass filtered, and reduced to its real part for reconstruction. [§11.4.3, Eqs. 11.78–11.80, Figs. 11.12–11.13]

A discrete-time random process is an indexed family of random variables. Strict stationarity requires all joint distributions to be invariant to time shift; wide-sense stationarity requires constant mean and autocorrelation dependent only on lag. [Appendix A, §§A.1–A.2.1, Eqs. A.1–A.24]

For an ergodic process, infinite time averages of almost every sample sequence equal the corresponding ensemble mean and autocorrelation, motivating finite-record sample estimates. Statistical independence implies uncorrelatedness, but uncorrelatedness does not imply statistical independence. [Appendix A, §§A.2.1–A.2.2, Eqs. A.12–A.31]

Autocorrelation at zero equals mean-square value, autocovariance at zero equals variance, and correlation magnitudes are bounded by zero-lag powers. For many processes covariance decays to zero and correlation tends to the product of means with increasing lag. [Appendix A, §A.3, Eqs. A.32–A.42]

The power spectrum is the Fourier transform of autocorrelation; its integral gives average power, and it is real/nonnegative (and even for real processes). Through an LTI system, output power spectrum is |H(e^{jω})|² times input power spectrum. [Appendix A, §A.4, Eqs. A.43–A.55]

For rational systems driven by white noise, output average power can be obtained from the zero-lag inverse z-transform of σ²H(z)H*(1/z*), turning difficult real integrals or infinite impulse-response energy sums into partial-fraction calculations. [Appendix A, §A.5, Eqs. A.56–A.71]

Butterworth lowpass filters are maximally flat and monotonic; their 2N magnitude-squared poles lie equally spaced on an s-plane circle, and the stable causal filter selects the left-half-plane poles. [Appendix B, §B.1, Eqs. B.1–B.3, Figs. B.1–B.3]

Chebyshev Type I filters are equiripple in the passband and monotonic in the stopband; Type II reverses that allocation. Distributing allowable error uniformly generally meets a specification at lower order than the monotonic Butterworth approximation. [Appendix B, §B.2, Eqs. B.4–B.10, Figs. B.4–B.5]

Elliptic filters are equiripple in both passband and stopband and minimize transition width for a fixed order and ripple specification; achieving both ripples requires finite-frequency zeros as well as poles. [Appendix B, §B.3, Eq. B.11, Fig. B.6]
pedagogy: A rigorous but engineering-oriented progression: definitions and transform pairs are derived carefully from periodicity, orthogonality, convolution, and z-plane arguments, then converted into flow graphs, computational costs, finite-word models, and measurement procedures. Proofs are algebraic and constructive rather than axiomatic; the text repeatedly gives two interpretations of the same result (periodic-sequence versus finite-record, time-aliasing versus circular convolution, STFT versus filter bank, direct spectrum versus autocorrelation). Examples are fewer but long and consequential, often carrying one set of data through several figures to expose a misconception. Chapters 8–11 contain 71, 53, 44, and 32 problems respectively, divided into basic problems with answers, further basic problems, and advanced problems; Appendix C gives answers to the first 20 basic problems of each chapter. Exercises emphasize derivation, proof, flow-graph tracing, algorithm design, numerical scaling, window selection, spectral interpretation, and counterexamples. The shard assumes mastery of earlier material on DTFT/z-transforms, LTI systems, sampling, FIR/IIR design, complex arithmetic, and basic probability; Appendix A is a concise probability/random-process bridge, while Appendix B supplies analog prototype facts. Because the PDF is a scan, the cached OCR is dependable for prose/headings but equations should be checked against the page image before verbatim reuse.

gems: Time-domain aliasing is taught as the exact dual of ordinary sampling aliasing: the same nine-sample sequence is periodically replicated with N=12 (no overlap) and N=7 (overlap), making Fourier-transform undersampling visible without abstraction. [§8.4, Figs. 8.8–8.9]

Two identical length-6 constant sequences convolve linearly to an 11-point triangle; wrapping that triangle modulo 6 visibly produces the circular convolution, while N=12 leaves it intact. [Example 8.12, Figs. 8.18–8.21]

In the 32-point DCT energy-compaction example, approximation error stays very small until roughly 25 coefficients have been removed: the 32-number decaying sinusoid is represented with only seven DCT-2 coefficients and slight error. [Example 8.13, Figs. 8.27–8.29]
For N=1024, the chapter contrasts N²=1,048,576 with Nlog₂N=10,240 operations—more than a two-order-of-magnitude reduction before further twiddle simplifications. [§9.3, discussion after Fig. 9.7]
The FFT historical aside traces the underlying algorithm to Gauss in 1805 and notes that Cooley and Tukey’s 1965 paper turned a long-known NlogN idea into a signal-processing revolution. [§9.1]

The Goertzel-versus-FFT decision is made concrete: when only M frequency samples are wanted, direct/Goertzel work scales as NM and can win when M<log₂N, even though it loses badly when all N bins are required. [§9.2]
The chirp-transform example extracts just 16 Fourier samples, beginning at 2π/27 and spaced by 2π/1024, from a 26-sample sequence by one causal convolution. [Example 9.1, §9.6.2]

Fixed-point FFT scaling produces a memorable rule: input-only scaling costs about one extra bit of noise-to-signal ratio per stage, whereas distributing a factor of 1/2 at each stage costs about half a bit per stage. [§9.7, Eqs. 9.65 and 9.69]
A 5 kHz-sampled spectrum needing bins no more than 10 Hz apart requires N≥500, so a radix-2 implementation chooses N=512 and obtains 9.77 Hz spacing. [Example 10.1, §10.1]

The sinusoid sequence deliberately separates spectral sampling from resolution: padding a 32-sample window to a 1024-point DFT draws a smooth curve but cannot split merged peaks; lengthening the window while retaining N=1024 actually resolves them. [Examples 10.5–10.8, Figs. 10.6–10.10]

A Hamming-window spectrogram of a linear chirp uses a 400-sample window and turns the increasing instantaneous frequency into a straight dark trajectory across time-frequency space. [Example 10.9, Figs. 10.11–10.12]

The utterance ‘Two plus seven is less than ten’ is analyzed twice: a 6.7 ms Hamming window exposes temporal/vertical voicing structure, while a 45 ms window resolves harmonics but blurs transitions. [Example 10.10, Figs. 10.17–10.18]

Actual Doppler radar data show a strong peak curving through clutter; simply selecting the largest peak in each DFT tracks a trajectory consistent with a spinning rocket fin alternately moving toward and away from the antenna. [Example 10.11, Fig. 10.19]

Four pseudorandom white-noise periodograms with L=16, 64, 256, and 1024 become more rapidly jagged as L grows but never settle toward the flat true spectrum—the visual proof that the raw periodogram is not consistent. [§10.6.2, Fig. 10.20]
Welch’s half-window overlap nearly doubles the number of sections and almost halves estimator variance, but greater overlap stops helping because adjacent records cease to be independent. [§10.6.3]

The quantization-noise case study compares 8-bit and 3-bit quantization of the same speech: 8-bit error is nearly uncorrelated and within about −1.10 to +1.63 dB of flat after smoothing, while 3-bit error visibly follows the speech and its spectrum is unmistakably shaped. [§10.7.2, Figs. 10.26–10.30]

Increasing the 8-bit quantization record from 2,000 to 14,000 samples predicts a sevenfold variance reduction; the measured autocorrelation bounds tighten from roughly ±0.056 to about ±0.025, matching the theory. [§10.7.2, Figs. 10.27–10.28]

Two nearly equal Kaiser-window Hilbert designs expose a hardware tradeoff: the M=18 Type-III design needs only five multiplications per sample because alternate coefficients vanish, while the M=17 Type-IV design needs eight but covers frequencies near Nyquist. [Example 11.4, Figs. 11.7–11.8]

The bandpass-sampling construction fits M=5 shifted copies of a one-sided analytic spectrum into one 2π interval, enabling fivefold complex decimation without aliasing and subsequent exact reconstruction. [§11.4.3, Figs. 11.12–11.13]

Appendix A turns a difficult infinite sum or real frequency integral for second-order IIR output noise into a straightforward partial-fraction calculation of the zero-lag inverse z-transform, ending in a compact closed form. [Example A.2, Eqs. A.67–A.71]
